name: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA)

card.summary: Surgery that moves both jaws forward, established as a sleep-apnoea operation and marketed online as a looks-plus-airway upgrade.
card.aka: MMA, bimaxillary advancement, Bi-Max, maxillomandibular osteotomy (MMO)
card.note: The strong evidence is for sleep apnoea, not appearance; lower-facial numbness is very common early on and hardware removal is reported in a fifth of patients.

quick.overview:
Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) is jaw surgery in which the upper and lower jaws are both cut and moved forward, enlarging the space behind the tongue and soft palate. It was developed within orthognathic surgery and is now one of the most studied surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnoea, usually considered after other treatments such as CPAP or other sleep surgery have not worked.

In looksmaxxing communities, MMA and bimax are discussed as a way to advance the face and sometimes to fix breathing at the same time, with threads about rotation, midface expansion and surgeon choice. Sleep-apnoea outcomes are well documented in meta-analyses; evidence on cosmetic outcomes is much thinner.
quick.mechanism: A Le Fort I osteotomy frees the upper jaw and a mandibular osteotomy, typically a sagittal split, frees the lower jaw; both are advanced and fixed with plates and screws. Advancing the skeleton also pulls forward the soft tissues attached to it, widening the airway at the palate and tongue base.
quick.risks: A 2025 meta-analysis found early lower-facial numbness in about 83 percent of patients, persisting beyond a year in about a third, and hardware removal in about 22 percent. Other documented concerns include bleeding, airway swelling after surgery, relapse, jaw-joint problems and a longer recovery than other sleep surgeries.

lead: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA), also called bimaxillary advancement or Bi-Max, is a jaw operation that moves both the upper jaw and the lower jaw forward.[1] It originated in orthognathic surgery for facial skeletal deformity and bite problems and was later applied to obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), where it is classed as a type of sleep surgery.[1]

For sleep apnoea, MMA is described in reviews as one of the most effective surgical options and a gold-standard surgical choice for refractory disease.[1][5] A 2025 meta-analysis of 31 studies and 1,597 patients reported a mean fall in apnoea-hypopnoea index of about 42 events per hour, alongside high rates of lower-facial numbness and of hardware removal.[3] The procedure is typically considered after other treatments have failed and requires a longer recovery than other sleep surgeries because the facial bones must heal.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities, MMA is mentioned as a surgery that may combine facial advancement with an airway benefit, and users discuss how it interacts with other procedures such as maxillary expansion.[14] Research on its cosmetic effects is limited compared with its sleep-apnoea literature.
infobox: Le Fort I maxillary osteotomy plus mandibular osteotomy, often with genioglossus advancement
Usually after nasal, palatal or tongue surgery or PAP therapy has failed (as described in reviews)[1]

paras: MMA enlarges the upper airway by physically moving the facial skeleton forward, taking the soft palate, tongue and surrounding muscles with it.[3] It is often performed with genioglossus advancement, which pulls the tongue base forward.[1] In the Stanford protocol of sleep surgery, MMA is described as the second phase of treatment.[2]
Technology such as virtual surgical planning and 3D printing has made planning more efficient, and a surgery-first approach has grown in popularity for malocclusion cases.[5]

Wikipedia reports that advancing the lower jaw was observed to reduce sleepiness in three patients in the late 1970s, which led to later use of MMA for obstructive sleep apnoea.[1] An AI-generated encyclopedia summary credits Riley and Powell at Stanford with a 1986 study showing larger posterior airway gains from two-jaw advancement than from mandibular advancement alone.[15]

Published case series from the late 1980s and 1990s reported MMA outcomes in sleep apnoea, including 23 patients treated with Le Fort I and sagittal split osteotomies with rigid fixation and a series of 50 consecutive patients treated as a site-specific approach.[10][11]

A 2010 systematic review and meta-analysis estimated clinical efficacy and safety of MMA from 53 reports describing 22 patient populations and 627 adults.[7] A broader 2010 meta-analysis assessed several upper airway surgeries including MMA for adult sleep apnoea.[6] A 2016 meta-analysis using individual patient data identified criteria associated with surgical outcomes.[4]

The 2025 meta-analysis found significant improvements in apnoea-hypopnoea index, respiratory disturbance index, lowest oxygen saturation and Epworth sleepiness scale, with a small reduction in body mass index.[3] A randomised trial compared MMA with autotitrating positive airway pressure in adults with severe sleep apnoea.[8] A narrative review describes MMA as a possibly unique treatment option with a high probability of cure while describing mandibular advancement devices as a solid option for milder disease.[9]

Human studies are mainly in sleep apnoea. They include the meta-analyses above, a randomised trial of MMA versus autotitrating positive airway pressure,[8] a clinical trial of how counter-clockwise rotation of the occlusal plane affects mandibular advancement, pharynx shape and polysomnography,[12] and registered studies of quality of life, airway volume and velopharyngeal function after MMA.[13]

Studies of appearance after MMA in non-sleep-apnoea patients were not identified; a review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea reports that many patients describe a positive change in facial aesthetics.[2]

In the 2025 meta-analysis the most frequent sequelae were early lower-facial numbness (about 83 percent), later numbness (about 67 percent before one year and 33 percent beyond one year) and hardware removal (about 22 percent); higher preoperative body mass index correlated with longer hospital stay.[3] Reviews also describe airway monitoring after surgery and complications specific to MMA that are weighed against its benefit.[5][2]

On looksmax.org, MMA appears in threads that ask how the operation affects other facial changes, for example whether it would undo cheek width gained from maxillary skeletal expansion; users in the thread name surgeons and share opinions without published data to support them.[14]

timeline.event: Lower-jaw advancement is observed to reduce sleepiness in three patients, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Riley and Powell at Stanford report greater airway gains from two-jaw advancement, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[15]
A series of 23 patients with sleep apnoea treated by MMA with rigid fixation is published.[10]
A series of 50 consecutive patients treated with MMA is published.[11]
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses pool MMA outcomes for sleep apnoea.[6][7]
A meta-analysis of 31 studies reports AHI improvement and common sequelae.[3]

lore.intro: MMA is discussed on forums mostly as part of broader jaw-surgery planning, with questions about interaction with maxillary expansion and surgeon choice.[14]

claims.claim: MMA after skeletal expansion could cause the cheeks to drop and lose expansion gains.
claims.believers: A forum poster who had miniscrew-assisted expansion asks whether later MMA will cost them cheek gains.[14]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified that examine MMA after maxillary skeletal expansion for cheek appearance; the sleep literature discusses maxillary expansion as a separate emerging option within MMA planning.[2]

claims.claim: Moving both jaws forward gives a looks improvement together with an airway benefit.
claims.believers: Forum discussions describe jaw advancement as serving appearance and breathing at once.[14]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses document large reductions in apnoea-hypopnoea index after MMA in OSA patients, and a review reports that many patients also describe an aesthetic improvement.[2][3]
